content: Centaurea solstitialis, commonly known as yellow starthistle, golden starthistle, yellow cockspur, or St. Barnaby’s thistle, is a plant species belonging to the Asteraceae family. It is native to the Mediterranean region. Since its introduction to North America in the mid-19th century, it has become a highly invasive and noxious weed, now covering over 18 million acres (73,000 km²) in the United States alone. Yellow starthistle is a thorny winter annual plant within the knapweed genus. It is characterized by its grayish-green appearance and multiple rigid stems that radiate outward from the base, forming a bushy cluster. This plant can grow up to two meters in height and even greater in diameter. It produces bright yellow flowers surrounded by long, sharp spines. The plant grows rapidly and is highly competitive. Its deep taproot, which can extend up to one meter into the soil, allows it to thrive in hot, dry summers. It exhibits remarkable adaptability, producing smaller plants with fewer seeds during drought years or when soil moisture is low. In its native Eurasian habitat, yellow starthistle is a normal component of the ecosystem, where it is controlled by natural enemies and co-evolved plant species. However, it was introduced to the United States in the mid-1800s as a contaminant in alfalfa seed shipments. Once dispersed into agricultural fields in California, it quickly established itself in the Mediterranean-like climate. Human activities such as mowing, grazing by domestic animals, and cultivation of wildlands facilitated its spread. Today, it is a common sight in pastures, fields, vacant lots, and along roadsides, particularly in the western United States, with California and the Pacific Northwest being the most heavily affected regions. Yellow starthistle is capable of forming dense, monotypic stands in fields, effectively outcompeting and preventing the growth of other plant species. Entire fields dominated by yellow starthistle are not uncommon. Its growth plasticity, competitive nature, preference for Mediterranean climates, and lack of natural enemies in its introduced range make it a highly successful invasive species. It poses significant challenges in agricultural fields, prevents grazing by domestic animals in rangelands, acts as a physical barrier to wildlife movement, and is toxic to horses. Control of yellow starthistle is challenging due to its resistance to certain removal methods. Its long root system makes it resistant to mowing, and its seeds can survive fire, rendering burning ineffective. However, biological pest control programs have shown promise in managing this invasive species. Six types of seed-feeding insects have been identified as effective against yellow starthistle. 1. Yellow starthistle bud weevil (Bangasternus orientalis): This fuzzy brown weevil lays its eggs in the flowers. When the larvae hatch, they feed on the developing seeds. 2. Yellow starthistle hairy weevil (Eustenopus villosus): This long-snouted, hairy weevil deposits a single egg inside each flower bud. The larvae consume the seeds within the bud. 3. Yellow starthistle flower weevil (Larinus curtus): This brownish weevil lays eggs in the flowers while feeding on pollen. The larvae hatch and consume the seeds. Additionally, three species of tephritid fruit flies target the seedheads of yellow starthistle: Yellow starthistle peacock fly and false peacock fly (Chaetorellia australis and Chaetorellia succinea): These small nectar-feeding flies lay eggs in the seedheads. Their larvae consume the seeds and flower ovaries. Banded yellow starthistle gall fly (Urophora sirunaseva): This fly produces larvae that pupate within a woody gall inside the flower, disrupting seed production. Furthermore, a variety of the rust fungus Puccinia jaceae has shown potential as a biological control agent. This rust fungus causes widespread pathology in the leaves of yellow starthistle, slowing its growth and reducing its ability to spread.
